In agency practice, it is useful to stop discussing a website as a “launch project” and start discussing it as an asset class. This changes sales, delivery, and client expectations. And, more importantly, it reduces the number of conflicts after release.

- The clearest test I have come across is this: if you stop advertising, what remains? If all that remains is a beautiful interface, then the client did not buy an asset, but an expense. If what remains is data, an indexable structure, an accumulated layer of reputation, working forms, integrations, and real manageability, then there is already a foundation for compounding effect. It is useful for an agency to make this explicit before the contract is signed.
- The next level is the zone of responsibility. A contractor really can be responsible for page architecture, analytics, access handover, performance, documentation, and stable support. But they do not control the quality of the offer, the response speed of the sales department, pricing policy, or the full media mix. When an agency promises a business result without these inputs, it is building its communication on an inaccurate foundation.
- The third point is infrastructure maturity. A good website does not only attract; it also reduces operational load: it routes leads into the CRM, helps standardize information, simplifies contractor replacement, and improves machine readability for new search interfaces. At that point, it is no longer just a “marketing website,” but part of the company’s system.

How do you articulate to clients the difference between website development and creating a digital asset?
